subject: math
verificationNotes: Hand-authored; numeric answers checked with sympy.
intro: A function $f$ is continuous at $x=a$ when three conditions hold: $f(a)$ is defined, $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ exists, and $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=f(a)$. If any fails, $f$ is discontinuous there. A removable discontinuity is a hole (the limit exists but disagrees with, or replaces, the value); a jump discontinuity has unequal one-sided limits; an infinite discontinuity has a vertical asymptote. The Intermediate Value Theorem says a function continuous on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.

items.prompt: Is $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}$ continuous at $x=1$? Classify any discontinuity.

steps: Check $f(1)$: the denominator is $0$, so $f(1)$ is undefined, and condition one fails.
Check the limit: $\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1\to 2$, so the limit exists and equals $2$.
The limit exists but the value is missing, so the discontinuity is removable (a hole at $(1,2)$).
solution.answer: Discontinuous at $x=1$; removable hole, since $\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)=2$ but $f(1)$ is undefined.

items.prompt: Find $k$ so that $f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2 & x\le 3\\ kx-3 & x>3\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=3$.

steps: Left-hand limit: $\lim_{x\to 3^-} x^2 = 9$, which also equals $f(3)=9$.
Continuity requires the right-hand limit to equal $9$: $3k-3=9$.

items.prompt: Use the IVT to show $f(x)=x^3+x-1$ has a root in $[0,1]$.

steps: $f$ is a polynomial, hence continuous on $[0,1]$.
Since $f$ is continuous and changes sign, the IVT guarantees some $c$ in $(0,1)$ with $f(c)=0$.
solution.answer: A root exists in $(0,1)$ because $f(0)<0<f(1)$ and $f$ is continuous.

steps: As $x\to 2$ the denominator approaches $0$ and $|f|$ grows without bound.
The one-sided limits are $\pm\infty$, so this is an infinite discontinuity (vertical asymptote $x=2$).

items.prompt: Is $f(x)=\begin{cases}x+1 & x<0\\ x-1 & x\ge 0\end{cases}$ continuous at $x=0$?

steps: The one-sided limits differ, so there is a jump discontinuity; $f$ is not continuous at $0$.
solution.answer: No; jump discontinuity (left limit $1$, right limit $-1$).

items.prompt: Does $f(x)=x^2-4x$ take the value $-3$ somewhere on $[0,4]$? Justify with the IVT.

steps: Since $-3$ is between $f(2)=-4$ and $f(0)=0$, the IVT guarantees a value of $-3$ on $[0,2]$.
solution.answer: Yes; $-3$ lies between $f(2)=-4$ and $f(0)=0$, so the IVT applies.
